deploy waits for test · protected environment → reviewers

props.title: What else a workflow can publish

items.d: Push a tag → release notes + binaries attached
Build & push to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR)
Publish to npm, PyPI, Maven — or GitHub Packages
Build a docs site and deploy it on every merge
Signed proof of which workflow + commit built this file

captions: Part seven. Deployment.
CI proves the code works. CD puts it in
front of users. Let's ship safely.

Here's a classic pipeline. Build, test, deploy to
staging,
then production.

Each deploy job targets an environment. Environments
are named
targets, with their own secrets and their own rules.

Production has required reviewers. The run pauses
here, and
waits for a human to approve.
You can also add a wait timer, and restrict
which branches may deploy.

Once approved, the job continues, and GitHub records
the
deployment, with a link to the live site.
Automation does the work. A human keeps the final
say.
What if two pushes land a minute apart? Two
deploys could race each other.
The concurrency key fixes this. Runs that share a
group name never run at the same time.
Add cancel in progress, and a newer run cancels
the older one.

Watch: four pushes arrive. Without concurrency, four
deploys overlap.
With it, only the latest one finishes.
For pull requests, use the branch name as the
group. Every new push cancels the stale run, and
saves minutes.

To deploy to a cloud, your workflow needs
credentials.
The old way was to paste a long-lived cloud
key into secrets.
If that key leaks, it works for anyone, for
months.
The modern way is OpenID Connect, or OIDC.
The job asks GitHub for a signed token that
says: I am this repo, on this branch, in
this environment.
AWS, Azure or Google Cloud checks that token against
a trust policy you wrote, and hands back credentials
that expire within the hour.
No stored cloud keys at all. To allow it,
give the job the id-token write permission.
Let's put the last few chapters together in one
file.
It triggers on every push to main.

Permissions are read-only, plus id-token write for
OIDC. And

the concurrency group means only one production
deploy runs
at a time.
The test job simply calls our reusable CI workflow.

Deploy needs test, and targets the production
environment —
so the required reviewers must approve.
Then it checks out the code, logs in to
AWS through OIDC with no stored keys, and runs
the deploy script.
Sixteen lines, and nearly every idea so far is
in there.
Deployment isn't just servers.
Actions can publish a GitHub release, with notes and
binaries, whenever you push a tag.
It can build container images and push them to
the GitHub Container Registry.
It can publish packages to npm, PyPI or Maven.
It can build a docs site and deploy it
to GitHub Pages.
And it can sign what it builds with artifact

attestations — proof of exactly which workflow, from
which
commit, produced this file.
